response.title: How long will a power station run a jobsite table saw for a day of framing and trim cuts?
response.answer:
For a typical 15-amp jobsite table saw, a portable power station with 2,000–3,000 Wh of battery capacity can often handle a full 8-hour workday of intermittent framing and trim cuts.

The key is that a table saw doesn't run continuously. You might spend 8 hours on site but only have the blade spinning for 30–90 minutes total.

Estimated runtime by power station size

Assuming a 15A, 120V jobsite saw drawing an average of 1,200W while cutting, with 85% inverter efficiency:

These are estimates, not guaranteed runtimes. Cutting thick lumber or hardwood can increase power consumption significantly.

How much battery does an 8-hour day actually need?

Estimated energy use by workload

1,000–2,000 Wh

Heavy ripping and framing

2,000–3,500 Wh

Illustrative battery consumption ranges for an 8-hour day, including inverter losses.
The catch: startup surge power

Battery capacity isn't the only consideration. A 15A table saw may draw around 1,500–1,800W under substantial load, with a much higher momentary surge at startup.

Look for a power station with:

2,400W or higher continuous AC output, preferably.

3,500–5,000W surge capability, although some saws may need more.

Pure sine wave inverter.

At least 2,000 Wh capacity for a typical day.

A 3,000 Wh power station with only a 1,800W inverter might have enough energy for the day but still trip when starting the saw or cutting demanding material. Published surge ratings also don't guarantee compatibility with every motor.

My recommendation

For an 8-hour framing and trim day, I'd target 3,000–4,000 Wh with a 2,400W+ inverter to provide a useful margin, assuming you're not also powering a compressor, dust extractor, or other tools.

Two questions would help me give you a much more accurate estimate:

What table saw are you using? (DeWalt DWE7491RS, Skilsaw, Bosch, SawStop, etc.)

Which power station are you considering? (EcoFlow, Bluetti, Anker, Jackery, etc.)

With those models, I can estimate how many cuts or hours of intermittent work you can realistically expect.
